title: Mixtape and Locker
premise: Quentin Nystrom, a debate champion counting the days until graduation, discovers that her late grandmother's recipe box holds more than cardamom and flour — tucked between recipes are instructions for maintaining the Lock, an old agreement that has kept the town of Halloway fed, sheltered, and strangely prosperous for a century. When Quentin's careless half-reading breaks one of the terms, the town's luck begins to rot overnight, and she learns her grandmother was the last Keeper. To restore what she broke, Quentin must finish the tradition her grandmother left unfinished — a final recipe requiring something Quentin isn't sure she can give — before the last jar in the pantry runs empty at graduation. In the end she pays the price willingly, inherits the Keeper's role on her own terms, and finally wins the argument at home by refusing to have it.
about_author: Ansel Marchetti grew up above his family's bakery in a small river town where every holiday had a required dish and no one asked why. He writes young adult fiction about kids who inherit things they never agreed to carry.

chapters.title: Ninety-One Days
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Senior year opens with a countdown calendar taped inside her locker and a screaming match with her mother about college applications she refuses to discuss. At debate practice she dismantles an opponent effortlessly, then goes home to lose the same argument at her own kitchen table. Beat: restless dread disguised as ambition.

chapters.title: The Recipe Box
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Clearing out her grandmother's pantry, Quentin finds the tin recipe box and notices cards that read like ritual: measurements in odd units, ingredients no store sells, warnings written in her grandmother's hand. One card, half-read, gets tried as a joke. That night, every light in Halloway flickers at 9:14 exactly. Beat: curiosity curdling into guilt.

chapters.title: Rot
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The town sours fast — bread won't rise, wells taste of iron, the harvest fair's prize pumpkins collapse. Only Quentin connects it to the card she burned through too quickly. Her best friend Priya catches her sneaking back to the pantry and forces her to confess. Beat: isolation breaking; the first ally.

chapters.title: Keeper's Terms
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Researching in the historical society basement, they find the Lock's origin: in 1924 the founding families traded a yearly offering for the town's survival, and a Keeper from each generation maintained it. Quentin's grandmother was the last, and her final entries stop mid-sentence. Beat: awe and horror — the family secret is the whole town.

chapters.title: What Mother Knew
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin confronts her mother, who admits she walked away from the Keeper role years ago and swore Quentin would never be asked to pay its price. The fight is the book's emotional core: inheritance as burden versus belonging as choice. They part angrier than before. Beat: betrayal reframed as protection.

chapters.title: The Missing Ingredient
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Decoding grandmother's marginalia, they learn the final recipe requires 'what the Keeper loves most, given freely' — and the offering window closes on graduation day. Quentin quietly tests small sacrifices; each fails. Meanwhile the town's decay turns dangerous when the river starts running backward. Beat: rising stakes, ticking clock made physical.

chapters.title: Debate Club
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. At the regional championship, mid-round, Quentin realizes she's arguing both sides of her own life — keep the tradition or end it — and forfeits the match to race home. Her coach, an old friend of her grandmother, reveals he once helped a Keeper and knows the pantry's true door. Beat: identity crisis resolved into purpose.

chapters.title: The Pantry Door
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Behind the shelving lies the Lock itself: a cold room where a century of offerings sit preserved, including her grandmother's — a recording of her voice, singing. Quentin understands the price isn't death but memory: the Keeper gives up being remembered. She prepares to pay it without telling anyone. Beat: quiet, terrible resolve.

chapters.title: Graduation Day
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. As caps are thrown, the Lock fails fully — frost in June, the town going gray and silent. Quentin enters the room and offers herself, but the Lock rejects a coerced heart; only freely chosen love completes it. Her mother arrives, having decoded the same truth, and instead gives her own most-loved thing: her memory of walking away, restored and surrendered. Beat: climax — sacrifice answered by sacrifice.

chapters.title: First Card, New Hand
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The town thaws; no one remembers the gray hour except Quentin, Priya, and her mother, who now shares Keeper duties. In the emptied recipe box Quentin writes the first new card in her own handwriting — not a rule but an invitation, so the next Keeper chooses rather than inherits blindly. Final scene: she takes down the countdown calendar. Beat: belonging earned, survival priced, home chosen.
